title: Forced mode forgives the credit on a wake, so the stage-0 fixed dose is not fixed
scenario: wake() (backoff.py:311-322) sets c = 0 in every mode. The engine calls it from _bo_between, which runs for forced as well as active (engine.py:1094, 1479). The design says forced holds forced_duty from t0 to the end (§1.7; module docstring line 26), and stage 0 counts a forced run only if its measured duty (busy_share) is within ±0.03 of d (analysis/backoff.py:373). Each forgiven wake erases the unpaid debt of a between-generation pause, which is up to D x max_sleep_s busy-seconds, at most once per wake_min_s. I simulated it with a fake clock: 40 paced 50-ms launches per generation, 0.2-1.0 s of unpaced work per generation, 120 s, and a partner batch landing in every between-generation pause (the worst case; the real trigger is a new solver/cuOpt batch or a gap-unit improvement seen at a tick during the pause). Without wakes busy_share is 0.250 at d=1/4; with wakes it is 0.286-0.353. At d=1/8 it goes from 0.125-0.127 to 0.145-0.185, and at 1/2 from 0.500 to 0.507-0.554. On instances where cuOpt or SCIP posts often (sing44, comp21-2idx: 2 of the 3 duty-response instances), bof25 and bof12 can fail the sanity rule. Then the floor rule (b) and possibly D_Y (a) cannot be applied, or they are applied to a contaminated dose. tests/test_backoff.py:241-252 (test_one_forgiven_wake_per_window) uses forced mode as its fixture, so it pins this behaviour.
fix: In forced mode, count the wake but do not forgive. In wake(), after self.wakes += 1, add `if self.forced: return False`. The sleep may still end early, because the remaining debt is paid at the next in-call pace point and the long-run dose is unchanged. Alternatively, have _bo_between skip the wake break when bo.forced. Move test_one_forgiven_wake_per_window to active mode at a level >= 1, and add a forced-mode test where wake() never resets c.

The finding holds. Two corrections: rule (a) is not affected, and the defect is a conflict inside the spec rather than a coding slip.

Code: Backoff.wake() (src/itrea/ea/backoff.py:311-322) sets c = 0.0 and advances b_cred in every mode. Nothing checks self.forced. Its only caller is _bo_between (engine.py:1449-1489; the wake is at :1477-1481). step() calls _bo_between for every non-shadow mode, forced included (engine.py:1090-1096). So a forced run forgives its credit on a partner wake, at most once per wake_min_s. The test tests/test_backoff.py:241-252 uses mode="forced" and asserts c == 0 after the wake, so it pins this behaviour.

Spec: §1.6 of the design states the forgiveness with no mode exemption. The builder implemented it as written, and it is not in the stated-deviations list. But §1.7 defines forced as "a fixed duty forced_duty from t0 to the end", and the module docstring (backoff.py:26) repeats it. §5.1 then counts a forced run only if its measured duty is within ±0.03 of d. That check is applied at analysis/backoff.py:373 with DUTY_TOL = 0.03 (:77) on busy_share (:153-154). When partners post, the spec's own forgiveness works against its own sanity gate.

Why each wake forgives nearly the whole pause: next_poll was last set at the previous generation's step-1 tick (engine.py:2028). The pause's first slice therefore ticks at once (engine.py:1469-1475) and sees every partner batch, and every info-incumbent drop of at least materiality, that arrived during the whole generation. The wake fires at the start of the pause and erases the whole pause debt, not a random part of it.

CPU check: I drove the real Backoff class in forced mode on a fake clock. Each generation had paced 50-ms launches plus 0.3-0.6 s of unpaced work. The engine's tick and wake logic was copied, and the partner-event times came from real traces: the sing44 A9 pilot's cuOpt and SCIP sends and info incumbents, and comp21-2idx's A6 cuOpt and A0 SCIP incumbents.

| d | busy_share with the debt kept | busy_share with forgiveness | shift |
|---|---|---|---|
| ½ | 0.500-0.502 | 0.507-0.532 | +0.007 to +0.032 |
| ¼ | 0.250-0.252 | 0.271-0.290 | +0.019 to +0.040 |

On chromaticindex1024-7 a generation lasts about 40 s (the pilot logged 3 rclock records and one cuOpt send at about 65 s), and the simulation shows 0 wakes there. The exposure is rule (b). A sanity failure on sing44 or comp21 for bof25 or bof12 removes that d from qual_b (analysis/backoff.py:390-399). That can push D_min to ⅛ with a "shortfall", which changes L for stage 1. The kept debt is paid at the next in-call pace point, capped by max_sleep_s as today. The 'debt kept' rows above simulate exactly this (break, no forgiveness) and stay within 0.002 of d. Skipping the wake break in forced mode instead would delay the cuOpt relay and change what stage 0 measures on comp21. Also move test_one_forgiven_wake_per_window to active mode at a level of 1 or more, and add a forced-mode test that wake() never changes c.

The finding is not refuted. The mechanism is in the code and the spec contradicts it; only the size of the effect is overstated.

**The mechanism is real**
- `Backoff.wake()` (src/itrea/ea/backoff.py:311-322) sets c = 0 and moves b_cred up in every mode. Nothing checks `self.forced`.
- `step()` (engine.py:1089-1096) calls `_bo_between()` whenever the mode is not shadow, so forced mode reaches the wake test at engine.py:1475-1481.
- The wake trigger is easier to hit than the finding says. Besides a new solver or cuOpt batch, it fires when `inc_external` falls by at least materiality. `_solver_in` (engine.py:2047-2054) takes `inc_solver` from SCIP's info, so the EA's own post, accepted by SCIP, also counts as a "partner improvement". `_post` runs at the incumbent step late in the generation (engine.py:1810-1814), and the pause's ticks then see SCIP's answer.
- The in-generation tick happens only at the start of `_step` (engine.py:1108-1110), so `next_poll` is long overdue when a pause starts. The first slice therefore ticks at once, and almost no debt has been paid before it is forgiven.
- `tests/test_backoff.py:241-252` does pin forgiveness in forced mode.

**This contradicts the specification**
- D-018 line 26 and design §1.7 define forced as "a fixed duty `forced_duty` from t0 to the end".
- Stage-0 sanity (design §5.1; analysis/backoff.py:369-375, DUTY_TOL = 0.03) requires busy_share within ±0.03 of d.
- With F busy-seconds forgiven, busy_share ≈ d + F/120, so the error is one-sided (always upward).

**Traces show wakes will happen on the stage-0 instances**
- sing44 A9 pilot: 6 SCIP sends and 69 cuOpt sends, spread over about 11 five-second windows.
- comp21-2idx A3 classprobe: the EA posted 98 improvements in about 43 s, and SCIP echoed about 50 of them. At d = 1/4 or 1/8 nearly every pause would follow an accepted EA post.
- chromaticindex has no partner incumbent before cuOpt's first, so rule (a) is barely affected. Rule (b), which uses sing44 and comp21, is exposed.

**Magnitude check (CPU, fake clock, the real Backoff class with 50-ms paced launches)**
- I used per-generation unpaced work taken from the traces: about 0.1-0.4 s.
- At d = 1/4, busy_share went from 0.252-0.254 to 0.256-0.283.
- At d = 1/8, it went from 0.126-0.128 to 0.132-0.168. That exceeds ±0.03 when a wake follows every pause on short-generation (comp21-like) instances.
- At d = 1/2 the shift was small, +0.002 to +0.021.
- The finding's 0.286-0.353 at 1/4 assumes 0.2-1.0 s of unpaced work per generation and is the upper end. Its 1/8 range (up to 0.185) is somewhat high but comparable to mine (up to 0.168).

**Consequence and fix**
Even when a run stays inside the tolerance, forced mode gives the EA extra GPU exactly when partners are posting, so the stage-0 dose is not the fixed dose the design calls for. The proposed fix is sound: in `wake()`, return False before forgiving when `self.forced`, or skip forgiveness in `_bo_between` for forced mode. The sleep can still end early, because the remaining debt is repaid at the next pace point. The test at tests/test_backoff.py:241-252 should then move to active mode.

I would rate the severity as moderate rather than major, because the effect is a few hundredths of duty rather than up to +0.1 at 1/4.

title: Shadow mode drops a would-be escalation when a lead (or own-feasible) resets the ladder before the next generation boundary
scenario: In shadow mode the only update() call is at step() start (engine.py:1092): no _bo_pace, no _bo_between, and none in finish/record(). contribution() (backoff.py:252-279) resets b_last and the level through _full_duty without first running the ladder up to `now`. own_feasible() (backoff.py:248-249) does the same. So an escalation that falls due between two generation boundaries and is followed by a lead before the next boundary is never logged. Fake-clock run, shadow, patience_own_s=30: phase-Y tick exit at 0.3, own feasible at 10, generation boundaries at 15 and 30, material lead at 43. Shadow logs no escalation (escalations=0, first_escalation=None, busy_per_level {'0': 59.7}). The same events with active-like updates every 0.05 s log escalate at busy 40.0 -> level 1. M6 (analysis/backoff.py:644-654) then reports before_lead=False for a run in which the active rule would have stepped down 3 s before the first lead. Design §3 item 5 says this is exactly what the shadow control exists to show. M6 is reported only and is not part of mech_ok (line 655), so no pass/fail flips, but the diagnostic is wrong in the case it is meant to catch. Likewise, escalations due after the last step() boundary are never logged, because record() at engine.py:2406 does not run update().
fix: Minimal engine-side fix: in shadow, call `self._bo_log(bo.update(now))` immediately before `bo.contribution(...)` (engine.py:1524 and 1541) and before `bo.own_feasible(...)` (engine.py:1112). Also call it in finish() before `self.bo.record(...)` (engine.py:2406). Doing it inside contribution()/own_feasible() also works, but those then need to return the update records. This MUST ship together with the due-time dating fix (next finding). Once update() runs on the contribution path, the escalate event's trace `t` equals the lead time, and M6's strict `te < first_lead` gives a new false negative.

votes.reason:
I could not refute it: the code does what the finding says, and a CPU-only fake-clock test reproduced it.

**Where the ladder runs in shadow mode.** Only `step()` calls `update()` (engine.py:1091-1092). The other call sites skip shadow mode:
- `_bo_pace` is passed only when not shadow (engine.py:1314).
- `_bo_between` is active/forced only.
- The lead path does not call it: `_bo_incumbent` (engine.py:1514-1527) calls only `phase_y_exit` and `contribution`.
- The assist path does not call it: `_bo_assist` (engine.py:1541).
- The exchange tick does not call it: it calls only `phase_y_exit` (engine.py:2037).
- `finish()` (engine.py:2406) calls `record()`, which runs `_acc` but not `update()` (backoff.py:353).

**What a lead does.** `contribution()` (backoff.py:252-279) calls `_full_duty(b)`. That sets `b_last = b` and level 0 without first stepping the ladder up to `now`. Any step down that fell due earlier in the same generation is lost. This defeats the module docstring's own promise that a late shadow update "still logs when it would have happened" (backoff.py:33-34).

**Reproduced.** Settings: shadow, `patience_own_s=30`; Y-exit tick at 0.3, own-feasible at 10, updates at 15 and 30, material lead at 43.
- Shadow cadence: events y_tick, own_feasible, lead; `escalations=0`, `first_escalation=None`, `busy_per_level {'0': 59.7, 'Y': 0.3}`.
- Updates every 0.05 s: an escalate at busy 40.0 to level 1, and `busy_per_level {'0': 56.7, '1': 3.0, ...}`.

**Realistic in practice.** Generation lengths in the A9 pilot traces (`traces/raw/a9pilot`):
- sing44, a guard used in M6: 37 generations in 120 s, about 3 s each.
- chromaticindex1024-7: 3 generations, the first ending at 48.7 s and the later ones about 24-35 s.

So a lead in the same generation as a due step down is a few-second window on sing44 and most of a generation on chromatic. In those cases M6 (analysis/backoff.py:644-654, `first_escalation` at 197-205) reports `before_lead=False` when the active rule would have stepped down before the lead.

**Weak parts of the finding.** The `own_feasible` half barely matters. It is called at engine.py:1112 right after the `update()` at the top of `step()`, separated only by the exchange tick. The finish-time loss is also minor. Neither changes the verdict.

**Fix.** The proposed fix is sound: in shadow mode, call `update(now)` before `contribution` and `own_feasible`, and in `finish()`. As the finding says, it must ship together with dating the escalate event at its due time rather than the log time.

The finding holds. I confirmed it by reading the code and with a fake-clock run on the CPU. Scratch directory /tmp/borev-shadowlead was created and then deleted.

1. Shadow mode calls update() in only one place: step() start, engine.py:1092. The other two callers are _bo_between (1455) and _bo_pace (1498), and neither runs in shadow mode. finish() calls bo.record() at engine.py:2406, which runs _acc but never update().

2. contribution() at backoff.py:252-279 goes straight to _full_duty(b) at line 278. That sets level=0 and b_last=b without first advancing the ladder to `now`, so any step down already due at that point is dropped.

3. The lead comes late in the generation. _bo_incumbent (engine.py:1514-1527, contribution at 1524) is called from _new_incumbent (1793), which _after_survival calls at 1779 after the repair (_ls_run at 1292/1295). In shadow mode, any step down that falls due between the generation-start update and a material lead in that generation is lost.

4. The window is real, not theoretical. - The own_feasible sub-path hardly matters in practice. own_feasible is called at engine.py:1112, right after the shadow update at 1092, with only the exchange tick in between, so it can only lose a step down that falls due during that tick. Adding update() there is harmless but not load-bearing. The real defect is the lead path at 1524. The assist path at 1541 only runs inside _exchange_in, also at generation start, so it too is nearly covered.

title: Escalate records are dated at the late update time, and led-state escalations use λ̂ at that time, so shadow's would-be timeline is late
scenario: update() (backoff.py:205-219) dates an escalation's busy time as be = b_last + thr. Three things are still taken at the update's `now` rather than at be. (1) The engine's trace event `t`: trace.event stamps the logging time. (2) first_escalation.t = now − t0 (line 218). (3) The timeline wall column (line 331). M6 uses that event `t` (analysis/backoff.py:199-201, 653). (4) In led state, thr = patience() is evaluated with λ̂ advanced to the late b (line 205). τ only grows while no event arrives, so be comes out later than the busy time at which the per-pace rule would have crossed. Fake clock, 20 material leads at 1-s spacing, then silence: updates every 0.05 s escalate at busy 23.78 (then 27.78). A single shadow update 8 / 15 / 30 s after the last lead dates the first escalation at 24.83 / 26.97 / 33.73. In shadow, generation boundaries are the only update points, so the error is up to a generation in wall `t`, and up to about 10 s (bounded by patience_max_s) in busy_s for the led state.
fix: Put a due-time field on every escalate record: t_due = (now − t0) − (b − be). This is exact in shadow, where busy equals wall, and within one pace interval in active. Set first_escalation.t and the timeline wall column from it, and have analysis first_escalation()/M6 read t_due (or busy_s in shadow) instead of the event's `t`. For the led state at level 0, find the crossing rather than evaluating τ at the late b: λ̂ evolves deterministically between events, so scan busy time from b_last to b in pace-sized steps (e.g. 0.05 s). At each step, check s − b_last ≥ clamp(κ/λ̂(s)), and escalate at the first s that satisfies it.

votes.reason:
The mechanism is real, and I reproduced it on CPU with a fake clock: updates every 0.05 s escalate at busy 23.78, and a single late update gives 24.83 / 26.97 / 33.73. It is still not a defect. Each part is either intended behaviour or feeds no rule.

(1)–(3) `t` is the time the event is logged. That holds for every trace event (`trace.event`, trace.py:69), and `first_escalation.t` and the timeline wall column follow the same rule. The module docstring says the due time is carried by the record's `busy_s` (src/itrea/ea/backoff.py:36-37). In shadow mode `slept()` is never called, so `paused` stays 0 and `busy_s` is exactly the would-be wall time. M6 already reports both values (`would_escalate_t` and `would_escalate_busy`, analysis/backoff.py:651-653). The proposed `t_due` field would be `busy_s` under a new name.

The claimed effect on M6 cannot happen: its `before_lead` boolean cannot differ between `te` and `be`. For it to differ, a material first lead L would need be < L ≤ te. Any material lead before `te` goes through `contribution(L)` (engine `_bo_incumbent` → backoff.py:273-278) before the shadow `update(te)` at engine.py:1092. `_full_duty` then sets `b_last = L`, so any escalation recorded at `te` has be' ≥ L + τ ≥ L + 2. That leaves two cases: te < L (both say before) or be' > L (both say not before). `_esc_before_lead` is applied to the active arm, where `update` runs at every FJ launch.

(4) In the led state, λ̂ is evaluated at the late b. This makes `be` later than the exact crossing, but the loop condition (backoff.py:208-210) guarantees be = b_last + τ(b) ≤ b, the generation boundary. The spec (§1.7) says shadow mode "logs the would-be phase, level and escalations at generation boundaries", so the code already dates escalations at least as precisely as the spec asks.

Shadow escalations in the led state can only come after a material lead. Their timing is read only by reported fields: `bo_first_escalation_s` (build_runs.py:578), `seconds_per_level`, and M6, whose boolean does not change, as shown above. The stage-0 rules (analysis/backoff.py:320-500) read no escalation or level timing, and `mech_ok` is M1–M5 only. The one real point is wording: the docstring's "still logs when it would have happened" overstates the precision for the led state. That is a docstring fix, not a defect that changes any outcome.

Confirmed, but only the led-state part. It is minor and changes no verdict.

Real part, claim (4): backoff.py:205 calls _lam_to(b) at the update's busy time. In led state at level 0, line 207 then takes thr = patience() = clamp(κ/λ̂(b_update)), and line 210 sets be = b_last + τ(b_update). The rule as active mode plays it would escalate at the first crossing s* where s − b_last ≥ τ(s). Between events λ̂ only falls, so τ(b_update) ≥ τ(s*) and the logged busy_s is systematically late. The late τ can also leave b − b_last < τ(b) after a crossing has already happened, which pushes the record to a later generation boundary. I reproduced the finding's exact numbers with a fake clock (shadow cfg, phase P at 0, 20 material leads at 1-s spacing): dense 0.05-s updates escalate at busy 23.779 then 27.779, and single updates 8 / 15 / 30 s after the last lead date the first escalation at 24.833 / 26.969 / 33.731. This contradicts the module docstring (backoff.py:36-37), which promises that a late shadow update "still logs when it would have happened (busy_s of the record)". One correction: the error is bounded by patience_max_s − τ(s*), which can approach 38 s, not "about 10 s".

By design, claims (1)-(3): spec §1.7 says shadow "logs the would-be ... escalations at generation boundaries". The wall `t` of trace.event, first_escalation.t (line 218) and the timeline wall column (line 331) are the logging time by contract; busy_s carries the due time. In shadow slept() is never called, so paused = 0 and busy_s already is the would-be wall time. The proposed t_due field would add nothing: build_runs.py:578 already reads busy_s, and M6 already reports would_escalate_busy next to would_escalate_t.

No gate is affected:
- M6's before_lead (analysis/backoff.py:651-653) cannot flip from dating. Say an escalation is recorded at update time t_u ≥ t_lead. Then the lead's contribution() (or phase_y_exit("own") just before it, engine.py:1519) reset b_last to t_lead first, so its be > t_lead. Led-state escalations come after the first lead by definition.
- classify_ca/_esc_before_lead runs on bo1 (active), which updates at every pace point, so lateness there is at most one FJ launch. The proposed 0.05-s scan is not needed in active mode.
- What is affected is only reported numbers: M6 would_escalate_busy and bo_first_escalation_s for shadow runs whose first escalation is in led state, and the shadow timeline.

Fix: at level 0 in led state, find the crossing in [b_last, b] (step scan or bisection on s − b_last − τ(s), with λ̂ advanced to s). Alternatively, correct the docstring to state the approximation.

Separate issue, not part of this finding and not fixed by its proposal: in shadow, update() runs only at generation start (engine.py:1090-1092). contribution() (backoff.py:252-279) resets b_last without first flushing an escalation that fell due earlier in the same generation. If the first lead lands in the generation where a search/own escalation fell due, that would-be escalation is lost entirely. That is what would actually mis-answer M6's question.

title: Phase-Y expiry is dated at the update that detects it, so in shadow phase P and the would-be ladder start a whole generation late
scenario: update() calls phase_y_exit(now, "expiry") at the first update after yield_until_s (lines 202-203). It records y_exit.t = now − t0 and sets b_last = lam_b = busy(now). In shadow, the first update() is at the first step(), after begin()'s whole initial generation. Fake clock, shadow, yield_until_s=30, patience_search_s=75, no partner incumbent, updates at 48 / 96 / 119 (chromaticindex's gen-0 repair takes 48.31 s in A9): y_exit = {t: 48, busy_s: 48, reason: expiry}, and first_escalation = None. Under the rule, phase P starts at 30 and the search step-down is due at busy 105. Here it lands at 123 > 120 and is never logged. The `tick` exit in shadow also happens only at _step start (engine.py:1110). The design accepts computing the phase-Y exit afterwards from the partners' events, but nothing re-anchors the governor's ladder. In active mode the same late dating is bounded by the gap between pace points.
fix: On expiry, date the exit at its true time. Compute be = b − max(0.0, now − t0 − yield_until_s) and pass it to phase_y_exit as the exit busy time (an optional `busy` argument). Use it for _charge, _full_duty, lam_b and y_exit.busy_s, and record y_exit.t = yield_until_s. This is valid because no governor sleep can fall between the expiry and the detecting update: sleep_due caps phase-Y sleeps at the expiry (lines 294-295), and shadow never sleeps.

title: The stage-0 STOP verdict treats "no duty passed the sanity check" as "no duty protects cuOpt"
scenario:
Line 383 drops every d whose chromaticindex run fails the sanity check (`counts()`) from `qual_a`. When `qual_a` is empty, lines 438-441 print "STOP: no duty ... brings cuOpt's first chromaticindex incumbent within 2.0x ... MPS is the next candidate and needs Berk".

Scenario: bof25 measures S_first = 1.5, but its lane-steps ratio is outside [0.75, 1.5]·d. This is plausible on chromaticindex: cuOpt's earlier incumbent arms the cutoff row earlier and changes the EA's step rate (design §2.3). If the other duties also fail sanity, the report concludes that the mechanism cannot protect cuOpt and sends the project to MPS. The measurement was invalid; the mechanism was not shown to fail.

`rules['a']['not_counted']` is computed but the verdict never consults it.
fix: If `qual_a` is empty and `not_counted` is non-empty, print a verdict such as "INVALID: sanity failed for d in {...} (duty / steps ratio); their S_first = {...}; fix or rerun stage 0". Print STOP only when every d counted and none has S_first <= 2.0. Optionally apply the same distinction to the rule (b) shortfall note.

votes.reason:
The code does what the pre-registered rule says, so this is not a defect in the diff. The design note's §5.1 says "Sanity first. For the forced runs to count, each must have…" and then "(a) D_Y = the largest d … with S_first ≤ 2.0. If none qualifies, stop: no stage 1. The pacing mechanism cannot protect cuOpt's first incumbent; report it. MPS is the next candidate, and it needs Berk." "Count" is the spec's own test for whether a run belongs to rule (a)'s candidate set. If no counted run has S_first ≤ 2.0, then "none qualifies" holds by the spec's definition.

- **Code matches the spec.** src/itrea/analysis/backoff.py:383 (qual_a) and :438-441 (the STOP string) implement that rule verbatim. The STOP wording is the spec's text, not the builder's gloss. The module docstring at :20-21 states this reading explicitly: "a run that does not count cannot qualify its d".
- **The behaviour is intended and tested.** tests/test_backoff_report.py:143-147 (test_stage0_a_run_that_fails_sanity_does_not_qualify) checks it.
- **The sanity failures are not hidden.** The finding says not_counted is never consulted. print_stage0 consults the same data instead: :898-907 prints S_first for every forced arm whatever its sanity result, and :908-912 prints "sanity: NOT counted: <arm inst> (duty …, steps ratio …)" just above "VERDICT:". In the finding's own scenario, the reader sees "bof25 S_first 1.50" and "bof25 chromaticindex NOT counted (steps ratio …)" on the same screen. The --json output also carries `sanity` and `rules.a.not_counted`.
- **The action is the same either way.** There is no stage 1, bo1 is None so no config is written, and the next step needs Berk, who reads the report. Nothing automated branches on the verdict text.
- **The fix would break the fixed rule.** Printing INVALID instead of STOP would depart from a pre-registered rule in a tool whose contract is "nothing is chosen by eye".

The scenario can occur, because sanity depends on the data. But the claim that the implementation misclassifies is wrong, and "major" is unsupported. At most, the spec's STOP sentence could be reworded so that "no run passed sanity" and "a valid run failed" read differently. That is a note for the design author, not a defect in b292a55..22dbe96.

I could not refute it. The finding holds as stated, though the severity is overstated.

What the code does:
- src/itrea/analysis/backoff.py:383 keeps a duty in qual_a only if counts(arm, CHROMATIC) is true and S_first <= 2.0.
- Line 387 computes rules['a']['not_counted'], but nothing reads it. Its only uses are the two definitions at lines 387 and 402.
- The verdict block (lines 434-449) branches only on missing, d_y, yu, ps and shortfall. So when every duty with S_first <= 2.0 fails sanity, it falls into the STOP branch at lines 438-441. That branch states as fact that "no duty in {1/2, 1/4, 1/8} brings cuOpt's first chromaticindex incumbent within 2.0x of A6's", that "the pacing mechanism cannot protect cuOpt's first incumbent", and that MPS is next and needs Berk.

CPU-only reproduction: I used the test fixture tests/test_backoff_report.py::stage0_world, run under the rules and in a scratch directory since deleted. Settings:
- S_first = 2.5 / 1.5 / 1.2 for bof50 / bof25 / bof12.
- bof25 and bof12 on chromaticindex given a measured duty of 0.35 and 0.225 (outside ±0.03).

Output: rules a = {D_Y: None, qualifying: [], not_counted: [0.25, 0.125]}. The printed report shows S_first 1.50 and 1.20 in its table and the line "sanity: NOT counted: ...", then ends with "VERDICT: STOP: no duty in {1/2, 1/4, 1/8} brings cuOpt's first chromaticindex incumbent within 2.0x ...". That verdict sentence is false in a state the code can reach.

The design (§5.1) and the module docstring at line 21 say a run that fails sanity "cannot qualify its d", so the filter itself follows the spec. But the spec says nothing about the case where nothing counts. Its stated reason for stopping only holds when every duty was measured validly, and the builder's list of deviations does not cover this case. In the reproduced case the measured duty was 0.35 against a setting of 0.25: cuOpt was protected even though the EA ran more than configured. That points to a calibration or accounting fault to fix and rerun, not a mechanism that cannot protect cuOpt. MPS would not fix it.

The defect matters because the report's contract is "nothing is chosen by eye" (module docstring), so the verdict line is the decision. Here it states a wrong reason and sends the project to MPS and an escalation to Berk on invalid data.

On severity:
- The decision to run no stage 1 is right in both cases.
- The printed sanity line (lines 908-912) appears above the verdict, so a careful reader could catch the contradiction.
- The defect is a wrong reason and a wrong next step, not a wrong stop/proceed outcome. Moderate rather than major.

The proposed fix is right. When qual_a is empty, check whether any duty with a finite S_first <= 2.0 is in rules['a']['not_counted']. If so, print INVALID with each d's duty, steps ratio and S_first, and say to fix and rerun stage 0. Print STOP only when every chromaticindex forced run counted. The rule (b) shortfall note (line 449) could make the same distinction using rules['b']['not_counted'].

title: The shadow control loses a would-be step down when a lead lands in the same generation, and M6 compares the logging time instead of the would-be time
scenario:
In shadow mode the ladder is updated only at `step()` (engine.py:1091-1092). Material leads are processed immediately (engine.py:1794 calls `_bo_incumbent`, which calls `contribution`). In phase P, `contribution` resets b_last via `_full_duty` without first applying the steps already due (backoff.py:273-279).

I checked this with the real Backoff class and a fake clock: phase P from 10, an update at 30, a material lead at 65 and an update at 70 give `escalations: 0` and `first_escalation: None`, although the step fell due at 50. On ca, A3 generations already run about 20 s (max_generation_s 19.6-21.1 in the existing traces), so a would-be step down inside the lead's generation is often erased. ca is the instance where M6 and the class-(P) diagnosis matter most.

Second part: M6 (analysis/backoff.py:651-653) compares the `backoff` event's `t`, which is the logging time and up to a generation late. backoff.py:36 states that the record's `busy_s` carries the would-be time, and in shadow mode busy equals wall.

The effect is that M6 and build_runs' `bo_first_escalation_s` / `bo_escalations` under-report escalation before a lead, the very event the shadow arm exists to show (design §1.7, §3.5). bo1 is unaffected, because it is updated at every pace point.
fix: In `contribution` (and `own_feasible`), apply the ladder steps already due before resetting: run the escalation loop of `update(now)` and return or log those records, dated at their busy time. Alternatively, have `_bo_incumbent` / `_bo_assist` call `self._bo_log(self.bo.update(now))` first when the mode is shadow. In M6, `first_escalation()` and `_esc_before_lead`, use `busy_s` as the time for shadow runs.

votes.reason:
Not refuted. Part 1 is a real minor defect. Part 2 describes the code correctly, but it only changes a verdict once part 1 is fixed.

Code path:
- In shadow mode `update()` is called only at the top of `step()` (engine.py:1091-1092). The other two calls sit in `_bo_between` and `_bo_pace` (engine.py:1455, 1498), which run only in active and forced mode.
- Leads are handled in `_new_incumbent` (engine.py:1794), which comes after survival, near the end of the generation. That can be up to a full generation after the last shadow update.
- Assists come from verdict processing (engine.py:2278-2279).
- Both go through `Backoff.contribution`, which in phase P calls `_full_duty(b)` and sets `b_last = b` (backoff.py:273-279, 187-192). It never runs the step-down loop of `update()` (backoff.py:206-222) first, so a step that fell due between the last update and the lead is erased.

Reproduction: real `Backoff` class, default `BackoffCfg(mode="shadow")`, fake clock, CPU only.
- Setup: phase P from t=10 (tick), `own_feasible` at 10 (patience 30, so the step falls due at busy 40), `update` at 30, material lead at 65, `update` at 70.
- Result: `escalations 0`, `first_escalation None`.
- Add an `update(60)` before the lead and the result is two escalations, the first at busy 40.
- In the search state (patience 75) the step falls due at 85. A lead at 95 erases it the same way.
- The finding's "fell due at 50" does not match the defaults (40 or 85), but the mechanism reproduces with the correct numbers.

Why it is a defect: backoff.py:36-37 promises that "an update made late — shadow mode updates once per generation — still logs when it would have happened". Design §1.4 has the rule update at every pace point, and §3.5 and M6 exist to show "whether the governor would have escalated before each first lead". Design §1.7's "at generation boundaries" says where the shadow logs. It does not permit losing a step the rule would have taken.

Affected outputs:
- M6 (analysis/backoff.py:646-653, rows from the bo0 shadow runs) reports `before_lead=False` for an escalation that would have come before the lead.
- build_runs' `bo_escalations` and `bo_first_escalation_s` for shadow runs under-count.

Scope corrections:
- `classify_ca` reads the bo1 (active) runs (analysis/backoff.py:756-758). The class-(P) diagnosis is therefore not fed by the shadow log, contrary to the finding's framing.
- Active mode has the same gap, much smaller: between the last in-call `_bo_pace` and `_new_incumbent`.
- Part 2: the escalate event's `t` is the logging time (trace.py:68-71 stamps `now()` at the call; `_rec` carries no `t`). The summary's `first_escalation.t` is also `now - t0` at logging (backoff.py:218-219).
- On its own, part 2 changes no `before_lead` verdict today: an escalation logged after the first material lead has already been erased by part 1. Once part 1 is fixed it matters. Even now, `would_escalate_t` is reported up to a generation late (`would_escalate_busy` is right).

Fix:
- In `Backoff.contribution`, and in `own_feasible` when phase is P, run the step-down loop of `update(now)` before `_full_duty` / resetting `b_last`, and return those records dated at their busy time.
- Alternatively, have `_bo_incumbent` / `_bo_assist` call `self._bo_log(bo.update(now))` first, in both modes.
- In `first_escalation()` / M6 / `_esc_before_lead`, compare `busy_s` for shadow runs, where busy equals wall.
- None of this touches the default path (`self.bo is None`) or the recorded hashes.

No scratch files were created.

The main part of the finding holds. The second part overstates its effect.

Part 1 is confirmed by the code and by a fake-clock run of the real Backoff class.
- In shadow mode `Backoff.update` runs only once per generation, at engine.py:1091-1092. There is no `_bo_between`, no pace argument, and no other `update` call.
- A lead is processed in the middle of a generation: engine.py:1794 calls `_bo_incumbent` (engine.py:1514-1527), which calls `contribution` directly.
- In phase P, `contribution` (backoff.py:273-279) calls `_full_duty`, which sets `b_last = b` and the level to 0. It never runs the ladder loop of `update` (backoff.py:206-220) first.
- Run used: shadow mode, phase-Y exit at 10, own feasible at 20, so `patience_own_s` 30 puts the step due at 50; then update at 30, material lead at 65, update at 70. Result: escalations 0, `first_escalation` None.
- With an extra update at 52 (as active mode's pace points would give), the same run logs escalations 1 with `busy_s` 50.
- This breaks the module's own contract (backoff.py:36-37: a late update "still logs when it would have happened"). It also breaks the invariant stated in tests/test_backoff.py:147: "the dated busy times do not depend on how often update runs". That test never puts a contribution between two updates.
- So the shadow control (bo0) under-reports a would-be step down whenever it falls due inside the same generation as a later lead, and that window is exactly where M6 looks. The lost steps reach the summary's `escalations` and `first_escalation`, and from there build_runs' `bo_escalations` and `bo_first_escalation_s` (build_runs.py:578), plus M6's `before_lead` (analysis/backoff.py:644-654).
- The scenario is plausible: in the existing ca A3@rc1 traces, generations reach about 21 s (max_generation_s 20.86-20.95, about 21 generations per 120 s), and leads land mid-generation.
- Severity is minor. M6 is reported only, not a gate. The ca class-(P) diagnosis and the glass4/sing44 classification call `_esc_before_lead` on BO1 (analysis/backoff.py:714, 761), and active mode updates at every pace point, so neither is affected.

Part 2 is literally true but has no effect on the M6 verdict as the code stands.
- `first_escalation()` (analysis/backoff.py:197-205) does take the event's logging `t`.
- In shadow mode, though, an escalation is only logged at a generation start U, with be ≤ U. Any lead L before U resets `b_last` to at least L, so be > L. Any lead after U gives both te ≈ U < L and be < L.
- So `te < first_lead` and `be < first_lead` always agree, and M6 already reports `would_escalate_busy` (the would-be busy time) beside `would_escalate_t`.
- The switch to `busy_s` only becomes necessary once part 1 is fixed. Escalations would then be logged at the lead itself, and te ≈ first_lead would make the strict comparison fail.

Fix:
- In `contribution` (and, for consistency, `own_feasible`), apply the ladder steps already due by `busy(now)` before calling `_full_duty`. Factor the escalation loop out of `update` and return those records dated at their busy time. Alternatively, have `_bo_incumbent` / `_bo_assist` call `self._bo_log(self.bo.update(now))` first in shadow mode.
- Then compare `busy_s` against the first lead's `busy_s` in `first_escalation()`, `_esc_before_lead` and M6.
- Add a test: shadow mode, updates per generation, a lead between a due step and the next update; assert the step is still logged at b_last + τ.

title: M5's overrun check uses the EA summary's wall_s (taken after the final clean-up) against an absolute slack, so the EA's ordinary end-of-run time can fail M5
scenario:
`wall` is the EA summary's wall_s. engine.py `finish()` measures it after `lp_worker.stop()` and a final `_gen_record`. The slack is `max_launch_s + 0.25`, which is about 0.30 s with 50-ms launches.

Runs of the base configuration without any governor already exceed that: neos-960392 A3@cl1 s1 ends 0.317 s after stop.t (partner_end), and A3@tp1 s1 0.253 s. neos-960392 is a stage-1 guard, and SCIP proves it at about 20-30 s.

A bo1 run with the same end-of-run time fails M5, and the verdict becomes "DO NOT ADOPT: failed M5" although no sleep overslept the stop. Caveat: max_launch_s is not in the old traces, so the exact margin is unknown.
fix: Judge the overrun relative to the same (instance, seed) bo0 run: flag bo1 when its overrun exceeds bo0's by more than max_launch_s + 0.25. Or take the EA's exit time from its last generation or stop event rather than the summary's wall_s.

votes.reason:
The finding rests on a slack of about 0.30 s ("50-ms launches"). That premise is wrong. `max_launch_s` is the longest launch measured over the whole run (ls_fj_gpu.py:921-926, dt = tn - tl around each _k_steps launch plus its sync). It reaches the summary through engine.py:1328 and 2407. On the instances that matter it is well above 50 ms.

I estimated it from the launch profiles in the old traces: the largest gap between consecutive prof["t"] entries. Each entry is appended right after `max_launch` is updated, and pace time is already subtracted, so the estimate overstates the true value by a few ms at most.

1. **The finding's own example passes.** neos-960392 A3@cl1 s1: overrun 0.317 s against a slack of 0.125 + 0.25 = 0.375 s. A3@tp1 s1: 0.253 s against 0.116 + 0.25 = 0.366 s. A3@ad1 s1 (0.254 s) passes even with a 50-ms launch.
2. **No base run fails.** Of the 128 runs with launch profiles in traces/raw, none fails `wall - end_ref > max_launch + 0.25`; the smallest margin is +0.058 s. All 7 A9@a9p pilot runs (EA beside cuOpt, the same family as bo0/bo1) pass by at least 0.17 s.
3. **The large overruns without profiles have long launches.**
   - ca (A3 0.35/0.40 s, lps variants 0.59/0.78 s): launches reach 1.07-3.8 s in every profiled ca run (cl1/rc1/rc1d/tp1), so the slack is at least 1.25 s.
   - toguru A3@lp1 (0.685 s): its note "generation 2 cut short during the repair (budget)" is stamped 120.695, so the local search itself returned about 0.69 s late. `_should_stop` is checked between launches, so this was most likely one launch of about that length, which `max_launch_s` covers.

**The "after the final clean-up" clause.** `lp_worker.stop()` is terminate plus join on a worker that has already exited (LP state done or no_solution in every pilot A9 run), and `_gen_record` is host-side, so both add almost nothing. `wall_s` is counted from `wall_start` (engine.py:1038, set in `begin()` after t0), so it slightly understates the overrun; the check is lenient, not harsh.

**Residual caveat (not a code defect).** The slack covers the stop-poll latency (STOP_POLL_S = 0.25) plus one launch, but not the rest of the generation after the local search (evaluate, survival). That is why neos-960392's margin is thin. This tight criterion comes from the spec itself (design doc line 357: "one launch + 0.25 s"), and backoff.py:640-641 implements it as written. No base or pilot run exceeds it.

title: cuopt_t_first is capped at the budget (120 s) when cuOpt finds nothing, but S_first, rule (c), M2 and the floor seconds use it as a real time
scenario:
`metrics.time_to_first` returns T with `cuopt_t_first_event = False` when there is no checked cuOpt incumbent. The report reads `cuopt_t_first` without that flag at line 337 (A6), line 347 (arms, S_first), rule (c) at line 407, M2 at 549-550 and floor_seconds at 802.

Scenario: if same-day A6 finds nothing on chromaticindex, t_a6 = 120. Forced arms that also find nothing then get S_first = 120/120 = 1.0, which passes rule (a) and gives D_Y = 1/2 with yield_until_s = 240. In M2, "120 <= 2 x 120" passes for two runs with no incumbent. This is unlikely on chromaticindex (A6 found its incumbent at 8.6 s and 9.4 s on seeds 0 and 1), but the verdict would be silently wrong.
fix: Require `cuopt_t_first_event` to be True. Otherwise treat the time as missing or infinite: S_first = inf, and M2 fails unless both runs are censored and the case is reported. Report floor seconds as "none" rather than 120.

votes.reason:
The claim is correct as a code fact. It only changes a verdict when the A6 baseline is itself censored or slow, which is unlikely, so it stays minor.

Why it holds:
- `metrics.time_to_first` (src/itrea/analysis/metrics.py:274-280) returns `Censored(T, False)` when a trajectory has no checked incumbent.
- `build_runs._metric_cols` (src/itrea/analysis/build_runs.py:946-951) stores that as `cuopt_t_first = T` and `cuopt_t_first_event = False` for every run with a cuOpt role.
- src/itrea/analysis/backoff.py never reads `cuopt_t_first_event`. It reads the bare `cuopt_t_first` at line 337 (t_a6), line 347 (arm t_first and S_first), line 407 (rule c, through rd[...]["t_first_chromatic"]), line 549 (M2) and line 802 (floor_seconds).
- The author meant a censored time to count as missing. Line 348 is `s_first = t_first/t_a6 if _fin(t_first) and t_a6 > 0 else (math.inf if c is not None else math.nan)`. That `inf` branch is only reached when the cuOpt role is absent (the value is then NaN). A run where cuOpt found nothing reaches the ratio branch with 120 instead.

How far it reaches:
- A censored ARM is the plausible case: the pilot A9@a9p chromaticindex run had cuOpt's first incumbent at 65.3 s (traces/raw/a9pilot). Such an arm gets S_first = 120/t_a6, about 13 with A6 near 9 s. That is a lower bound on the true ratio, so rule (a) (≤ 2.0), the (Y) classification (≤ 3), and M2 (120 ≤ 2 x 9 is false) still reject it correctly.
- A wrong verdict needs A6's own chromaticindex value to be censored or ≥ 60 s. A6 found its incumbent at 8.556 s and 9.435 s on seeds 0 and 1 (traces/raw/classprobe).
- In that case the finding's arithmetic is right:
  - A censored forced arm gets S_first = 1.0 (or 120/t_a6 ≤ 2), which passes rule (a).
  - D_Y = 1/2 if that arm passes sanity.
  - yield_until_s = max(30, ceil(240)) = 240.
  - M2 passes 120 ≤ 240 although no run found an incumbent.
- floor_seconds is only reported; F is judged on dP at line 699. So it shows 120 instead of "none" but changes no verdict. cuOpt also finds krka and fhnw in under 1.1 s in every trace.

The defect is real but latent. The fix is cheap and matches the intent the code already shows: require `cuopt_t_first_event` before using the time. Treat an arm's censored time as inf in S_first, and a censored A6 as a missing baseline (stage 0 INCOMPLETE; M2 fails with a reported reason). Print floor seconds as censored rather than 120.

I could not refute it. The defect is real and the severity of minor is right.

**How a no-incumbent run is recorded.** `metrics.time_to_first` (src/itrea/analysis/metrics.py:274-280) returns `Censored(T, False)` when there is no incumbent at or before T. `summarize` stores this as `t_first = T` and `t_first_event = False` (metrics.py:317). build_runs then writes both under a `cuopt_` prefix (build_runs.py:107, 948-951). A CPU check confirmed it: `M.summarize([], 100.0, 1, 120.0)` gives `t_first = 120.0` with `t_first_event = False`, and so does a single step at t = 130.

**What backoff.py does with it.** It never reads `t_first_event` (grep finds no match). `RunView.get` (lines 115-117) maps only None and NaN to the default, so a censored 120 passes through as if it were a real time:
- Line 337 (`t_a6`) and line 347 (each arm's `t_first`) take it as is.
- The fallback at line 348 (`math.inf if c is not None`) shows the intent was "no time = infinite". That branch can never fire, because a censored time is the finite budget, not NaN.
- Rule (c) at lines 405-408 then sets `yu = max(30, ceil(2 x 120)) = 240`.
- M2 at lines 549-550 compares the two times directly: `tb <= 2.0 x ta`.
- `floor_seconds` at line 802 reports 120. This one is informational only: F at line 698 judges on dP, so only the report is wrong there.

**Wrong verdicts this produces:**
- A6 finds nothing on chromaticindex and a forced arm also finds nothing: `S_first = 120/120 = 1.0`, which passes rule (a). The result is D_Y = 1/2 and `yield_until_s = 240`, longer than the 120 s run.
- A variant the finding does not mention: A6's first incumbent comes at 60 s or later and the arm finds nothing. For example 120/70 = 1.71, which still passes rule (a).
- M2 passes with both runs censored (120 <= 240). It also passes when A6 found its first at 60 s or later and bo1 found nothing.

When A6 finds its first incumbent early (8.6 s and 9.4 s on seeds 0 and 1) and the arm is censored, the ratio is above 2 and the check fails correctly. That is why the case is unlikely in practice, but the verdict is silently wrong when it does happen.

The design (§5, line 305) does not say how a censored time is treated.

**Fix:** gate on `cuopt_t_first_event`.
- If it is False, use `t = inf` (A6's `t_a6 = inf` makes S_first undefined: report it, do not qualify).
- Rule (c) gets no value when `t_dy` is censored.
- M2 fails unless bo1's event is True and its time is within 2x A6's, or A6 itself is censored and that case is reported.
- `floor_seconds` reports "none" instead of 120.
